{"answer": "# Machine-learned surrogates for auger-powder calibration

**Bottom line.** For the described 3-mm-outlet doser, start with a **probabilistic emulator of measured DEM outputs**, not a pretrained particle simulator. A Gaussian process (GP), small neural network, or fitted response surface can map contact parameters and operating conditions directly to mass per revolution, tap release, afterflow, and no-flow probability. This is much cheaper to train than a full trajectory model and permits posterior uncertainty and targeted DEM runs. Particle graph simulators are promising if many related geometries or operating trajectories must eventually be simulated, but published speed and generalization results do **not** establish that an existing checkpoint predicts a tapped, intermittently flowing, SJKR-cohesive auger. Published granular examples also distinguish DEM-trained models from models trained on the material point method (MPM). (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000036, pqac-00000070)

## What has been demonstrated

| Approach | Training target and demonstrated scope | Generalization and relevance to the doser |
|---|---|---|
| **Particle graph simulators (GNS; “learning to simulate”)** | Construct nearby-particle edges; an encoder–message-passing processor–decoder predicts acceleration, followed by numerical position/velocity updates. Choi and Kumar trained a granular GNS on **MPM**, not DEM: 385 two-dimensional trajectories at five friction angles, 15°–45°, and 1,000 three-dimensional barrier trajectories. | Demonstrated different column configurations and barriers, and friction-angle-conditioned prediction within the studied setting. Their 2D training material had **fixed cohesion** of 0.1 kPa; this is not evidence for extrapolation over SJKR surface energy, rolling friction, moisture, or an auger outlet. (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000007, pqac-00000019) |
| **Mayr et al., Learning 3D Granular Flow / Boundary Graph Neural Networks (BGNN)** | **LIGGGHTS DEM** trajectories train a particle graph. Virtual nodes at nearby triangular-wall surfaces convey particle–wall distances and surface normals. Evaluations include hoppers, rotating drums, and moving-blade mixers; the earlier hopper study used 30 trajectories with varied wall angles, openings, and initial fills. Cohesive as well as noncohesive examples appear in the BGNN evaluation. | The authors tested **held-out changes to hopper outlet/wall angles and drum length**; Figure 5 displays predictions beside DEM ground truth for these out-of-distribution geometries. This is more pertinent to an auger than column collapse, but is **not** a test of a new contact law or reliable prediction of rare clogs. For one drum benchmark, 250,000 LIGGGHTS steps took **356 s on a CPU**, versus **158 s for 2,500 BGNN predictions on an A100**—different hardware and time resolution. (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000063, pqac-00000068) |
| **NeuralDEM, Alkin et al. (2025)** | A **DEM/CFD–DEM-trained field-based neural operator**: compress particle information into continuous fields and use interacting transformer-style branches for particle and, where applicable, fluid dynamics. Hopper data vary geometry and friction; a separate fluidized-bed model uses CFD–DEM. It predicts macroscopic drainage, transport, and mixing rather than requiring accurate individual-particle paths. | It handled withheld **combinations** of hopper angle and shear-cell friction angle within the studied range; this is parameter interpolation, not a verified new auger geometry or new SJKR physics. In its reported benchmarks, a 250,000-particle, 40-s hopper DEM run took **3 h on 16 CPU cores**, versus **1.4 s** for the fastest neural rollout on one GPU (**8 s** including all output points); a 500,000-particle fluidized-bed case took **6 h on 64 CPU cores**, versus **11 s** on one GPU. Training the fluidized-bed model used approximately **320 H100 GPU-hours**. These figures describe different hardware and exclude amortization of dataset generation. (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000014, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000023) |
| **Contact-memory graph networks (TRACE, 2026 preprint)** | Store evolving **contact-edge memory**, predict constrained normal/tangential forces, and train with single-step then rollout losses. Tested on 2D/3D column collapse against **MPM**, not an SJKR auger DEM. | Reports **8.9×–12.2×** speed relative to its MPM reference and improved deposit errors over graph baselines. Contact history is attractive for stop/start flow, but published tests do not demonstrate moisture, adhesive bonds, tapped walls, or inference of physical cohesion. (pqac-00000016) |
| **Low-dimensional DEM-output emulators** | Train directly on responses at deliberately chosen contact-parameter settings. Demonstrations include a quadratic D-optimal regression of repose angle, porosity, and flow rate for cohesive/free-flowing powders; a **symbolic-regression** metamodel fitted to **563 DEM parameter sets**, checked against 68 independent sets; and polynomial response surfaces for rotating-drum avalanche energies of AM powders. | Best matched to a small number of expensive auger outputs and Bayesian inversion. A fitted response surface is reliable only inside its sampled geometry, contact-model, environmental, and operating-condition domain; it does not automatically simulate particles or transfer to recoating. In the rotating-drum study, factor screening also eliminated weakly influential wall-contact parameters before fitting, illustrating why parameter identifiability should be assessed before expanding a design. (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000035, pqac-00000038) |

A **neural operator** learns a map between discretized fields, rather than rebuilding and stepping every grain-contact graph. NeuralDEM is a concrete granular example; it is not evidence that a generic Fourier neural operator, trained on unrelated fields, can resolve a 3-mm bridge or predict a zero-flow event. The granular-ML review specifically notes difficulties with changing particle contacts, solid-to-flowing transitions, and reconstructing physically admissible particle states from field representations. Thus, use a field operator if macroscopic fields over many operating conditions justify its training cost; retain contact-resolved DEM when clogging and tap-induced release determine the likelihood. (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000014, pqac-00000070)

## Inverse problems: what is known, and what is not

**Friction has been inverted with a differentiable graph simulator.** Choi and Kumar differentiated an MPM-trained GNS through a granular-column rollout and optimized friction angle against a target runout distance. Four held-out collapse cases gave inferred-angle errors **below 8.94%**; the authors report approximately **151×** faster optimization iterations than their MPM/finite-difference baseline. This estimates a continuum-model friction angle—not particle–particle sliding friction, wall friction, SJKR cohesion, or moisture from auger mass data. Differentiating long particle rollouts was memory-intensive and required checkpointing. (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000073)

**Cohesion-related and rolling parameters have been estimated with DEM response surrogates**, but an optimizer is not a Bayesian posterior. Katagiri and colleagues used GP-guided Bayesian optimization of a cohesion-related coefficient and rolling resistance against consolidation void ratio. A near-optimal result appeared within **12 optimization trials**; nevertheless, those calibrated parameters produced an **excessively cohesive spreading layer**. The authors attribute this to changed loading mechanics and stress scaling. Their GP guides evaluations toward an optimum; it does not by itself report a joint probability distribution of plausible physical parameters. For an actual parameter posterior, **GrainLearning** provides sequential Bayesian filtering of experimental time series against DEM runs and supports surrogate modeling as an alternative to repeatedly evaluating DEM. (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000037)

**Non-uniqueness is a substantive risk.** In a cohesive-powder study, different adhesion-energy/rolling-friction combinations reproduced the same repose angle, while matching unconfined yield strength called for a substantially different rolling-friction value. No single tested set reproduced both measurements consistently. A salt mass-per-revolution match without fitting is an excellent **forward check for that case**, but it is not evidence that the remaining powders’ contact parameters are identifiable from mean dose alone. (pqac-00000036, pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040)

## Recommended calibration and validation design

1. **Define the estimand as effective DEM parameters.** For each powder and batch, condition particle-size distribution, density, and measured moisture history; infer a *small, sensitivity-screened* subset of particle–particle sliding/rolling resistance, particle–PLA/PETG wall interaction, and SJKR cohesion. Treat fill level/packing history, powder shape, ambient humidity, and the tap impulse as recorded inputs or nuisance variables. Adhesive-energy and rolling coefficients depend on the chosen contact law and representation of particle shape; do not report them as uniquely measured intrinsic material constants. The finding that rolling friction can compensate for spherical representation of nonspherical grains reinforces this distinction. (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000036, pqac-00000066)
2. **Generate an auger-specific DEM design.** Sample physically plausible parameters and deliberately include both flowing and jammed regimes, each reservoir, low/high fill, tilt, 1–30 rpm, stop/start states, and housing taps. Export the *same balance-observable summaries* as in the laboratory, with replicate initial packings; reserve entire powder batches, operating conditions, and, if relevant, outlet geometries as held-out tests. A predictor of average mass per turn alone cannot be expected to learn afterflow or the no-flow fraction. The varied-parameter DEM datasets and out-of-distribution geometry tests in published work illustrate the need to include each intended axis of generalization in training and evaluation. (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000063, pqac-00000070)
3. **Fit a multi-output or linked likelihood.** A GP or small ensemble can emulate continuous mass-per-revolution, tap mass, and afterflow parameters; fit no-flow events with a Bernoulli/binomial likelihood and account for replicate variation. Compare posterior predictions to the **full incremental-mass traces**, not just their means. Include measurement noise, DEM-to-experiment discrepancy, and emulator uncertainty; acquire new DEM runs where posterior probability or uncertainty is high, especially near flow/no-flow transitions. These are proposed design choices for this doser, rather than published validation of an auger-specific surrogate. Bayesian filtering and documented cross-test failures motivate explicit uncertainty and independent checks. (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000070)
4. **Cross-check, do not force a universal flowability score.** Use **D7891 FT4 shear testing** and **D6773 ring shear** for constrained-strength information; **B213 Hall** and **B964 Carney** for funnel flow (including non-flow); **B212** apparent density and **B527** tap density for packing; **B214** sieving and **B822** light-scattering sizing for feed distribution. Include repose angle, documented humidity/conditioning and loss on drying. Report the actual apparatus, consolidation stress, sample preparation, and conditioning: these methods probe different stress and flow regimes. The source review’s summary table inconsistently groups some flow and density methods; its bibliography explicitly names **B964 as Carney *flow rate*** and **D7891 as Freeman powder *shear testing***, so those should not be silently relabeled as density or universal spreadability tests. (pqac-00000043, pqac-00000048, pqac-00000050, pqac-00000067)
5. **Measure spreadability separately.** For the AM-relevant metal powders, compare posterior-predictive rankings with a small recoater experiment at relevant blade/roller type, speeds and layer heights: image-based coverage and bare-patch frequency, layer mass/packing, thickness variability, and surface-height variation. Hulme-Smith and colleagues demonstrated inexpensive image-derived layer coverage over **50–200 mm/s** and **50–100 µm**; Yuasa and colleagues found AlSi10Mg surface-height variation increased markedly above **50 mm/s**, and powder-shape rankings changed at high speed. Angle of repose and FT4 basic flow energy can be informative correlates, but dosability through an auger, funnel discharge, and thin-layer recoating are *different operations*. The consolidation-to-spreading failure is direct evidence against declaring spreadability from a calibrated dosing fingerprint alone. (pqac-00000042, pqac-00000055, pqac-00000027)

At **26–30 CPU-min per revolution**, even 100 single-revolution DEM cases would require roughly **43–50 CPU-hours**, before initialization, extra turns, replicates, and tap/afterflow sequences. This is a planning calculation from the runtime supplied in the question, **not** a published benchmark. It favors factor screening, space-filling initial runs, adaptive acquisition, and a cheap summary-output emulator first. Use a wall-aware particle GNN later if those runs already produce sufficient resolved trajectories and the research question genuinely requires transfer between screw/outlet designs. The reported NeuralDEM inference speed should not be read as a prediction of its training or validation cost for this doser. (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000038, pqac-00000070)

## Public software and pretrained artifacts

- **NeuralDEM:** [github.com/Emmi-AI/NeuralDEM](https://github.com/Emmi-AI/NeuralDEM). The authors state that inference code, **pretrained model weights**, and one example trajectory for each hopper and fluidized-bed case are released; the complete approximately **3.2-TB** datasets are available on request. Those weights were trained for the published cases, not an auger. (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000061)
- **Choi–Kumar GNS and inverse examples:** [github.com/geoelements/gns](https://github.com/geoelements/gns) and [github.com/geoelements/gns-inverse-examples](https://github.com/geoelements/gns-inverse-examples), reported under MIT license. Their **training data and trained models** are deposited on DesignSafe; the paper lists dataset DOI **10.17603/DS2-4NQZ-S548** and inverse-example DOI **10.17603/DS2-0WJQ-0J84**. These are MPM-trained granular examples. (pqac-00000064, pqac-00000073)
- **Mayr BGNN:** [ml-jku.github.io/bgnn](https://ml-jku.github.io/bgnn/) is the documented project page with visualizations. The retrieved paper establishes this page, **not a verified downloadable pretrained checkpoint**; verify repository and license before planning reuse. (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000063)
- **TRACE:** [github.com/Data-Driven-Computational-Geotechnics/TRACE](https://github.com/Data-Driven-Computational-Geotechnics/TRACE) is documented as available code; a pretrained auger or DEM-contact-law checkpoint is **not documented**. (pqac-00000016)
- **GrainLearning:** an open-source Bayesian calibration/surrogate toolbox with published [JOSS software article](https://doi.org/10.21105/joss.06338) and [archived release](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.8352544). It is infrastructure for calibration, **not a pretrained powder-flow predictor**. (pqac-00000065, pqac-00000074)

**Assessment:** Existing open implementations provide useful architectures, calibration software, and some pretrained *benchmark* weights. None of the cited evidence establishes a transferable pretrained model for this doser’s PLA/PETG walls, rotating helix, SJKR adhesion, taps, and intermittent milligram-scale discharge. The experimentally defensible route is an auger-specific, uncertainty-aware inverse emulator, independently challenged by shear, packing, size/moisture, and actual recoating observations. (pqac-00000036, pqac-00000061, pqac-00000070)"}

## 1. fransen2026towardsscientificmachine pages 23-24 (Context ID: pqac-00000070)

e ML models are guided by physical constraints and scarce experimental data and complemented by abundant
simulation data. For example, ML can assist in defining appropriate strain energy density functions or yield surfaces in
stress space (augmented by other variables), rather than relying on handcrafted models developed by domain experts.
Symbolic regression can derive mathematical formulations directly from data, providing a middle ground between
black-box ML models and fully physics-based approaches. These constitutive model surrogates should be general
enough to cover both the solid-like (small strain, rate-independent) and fluid-like (large strain, rate-dependent) regimes
of granular materials, incorporating physical principles (or biases) through regularisation. Lastly, it is essential to
systematically verify ML-based constitutive surrogates by degenerating them into limiting cases, such as elastic solid
and Newtonian fluid behaviour and benchmarking them against them.


Learning field evolutions of underlying governing equations  Neural operators are capable of learning mappings
between functional spaces. They are promising tools for bypassing conventional numerical methods to solve governing
equations that have strong nonlinearity and discontinuity without the issues of numerical instabilities due to spatial/tem-
poral discretisation. These methods allow generalisation across different problem geometries and material parameters
without needing handcrafted theories at a specific length or time scale. However, when applied to granular materials,
neural operators face scalability issues due to the dynamic particle-scale interactions that exhibit macroscopic material
behaviour transitioning between fluid-like and solid-like. Future directions should focus on refining encoder/decoder
architectures to express spatial and temporal patterns in both the physical regime and on utilising transfer learning
techniques to specific engineering tasks, e.g., geometries, materials, etc. Learning the multi-scale features of gran-
ular systems relies on latent state representations that can handle strong discontinuity and nonlinearity at the lower
scales while capturing macroscopic fields of interest under various initial and boundary conditions. One example of
circumventing the scalability issue is training on the underlying fields instead of fine-grained particle kinematics and
interaction features in graph neural networks. However, the physically admissible microstructures, ready to be plugged
again into numerical solvers like DEM, are difficult to reconstruct.


Learning uncertainties from limited real-world data  Many engineering problems in industry involve risk assess-
ment and/or design optimisation, which integrate real-world uncertainty (although limited) into the physical processes
represented by their predictive models. Given the stochastic nature of granular systems and the variability in material
properties and conditions, uncertainty quantification is crucial in granular simulations and practical engineering applica-
tions. Data-driven surrogates, either based on classical machine learning or deep learning (see Sec. 4), are essential
in constraining uncertainties with real-world measurement data or design objectives (e.g. through Bayesian updating
and optimisation). Although deep learning models can learn to generalize across unseen parameter combinations, their
probability landscape over the parameters are very likely to be different from the counterpart of the numerical models,
adding additional uncertainties that are difficult to trace. A promising direction would be adding model uncertainties to
deep learning models (e.g. Bayesian neural networks). The stochastic behaviour in real-world applications could be
approached through ensembles: running multiple predictions with different parameters and averaging the results. Future
works should also include the trade-off between large and small neural networks for general or specific engineering tasks
to better use compute resources. Techniques such as Bayesian inference and Gaussian processes can be instrumental in
understanding the robustness of ML-based constitutive models and identifying part of ML predictions that might no
longer be reliable. By incorporating uncertainty quantification via the combined use of physics-based models and their
ML surrogates into digital twin applications, researchers can enable more informed decision-making for real-world
engineering processes.

Open science infrastructure to facilitate “GranML”  The importance of data quality, sharing and reproducibility
was discussed extensively in the workshop. For ML models to be broadly applicable and trusted by the community,
they must be developed using standardized datasets and workflows that ensure reproducibility against well-known
engineering benchmark problems. Open science practices can provide the infrastructure necessary for developing
models and data resources collaboratively. To facilitate progress, future efforts should establish community-wide
standards for data sharing and model benchmarking, such as the Open Network on DEM Simulations (ON-DEM) funded
by the European Cooperation in Science and Technology and DesignSafe by the US National Science Foundation.
An open-access platform akin to ImageNet could serve as a repository for training datasets, pre-trained models, and
evaluation metrics. Such a platform would not only improve reproducibility but also foster collaboration, enabling
researchers from different disciplines to contribute to and benefit from shared data and methodologies.

In addition to the topics addressed during the workshop and in this position paper, several broader challenges emerged
that are particularly relevant to machine learning for granular materials. These include issues of scalability when dealing
with large-scale systems involving millions of particles, the development of hybrid approaches in which physics-based
and data-driven models are used and the need for improved interpretability to obtain engineering insights. The potential
applications of ML models for granular materials extend far beyond civil and mechanical engineering. More accurate,
scalable, and interpretable ML-based approaches would also benefit fields such as pharmaceutical manufacturing, food
processing, particle technology, and agriculture. Progress in the research area addressed in this position paper and those
beyond will enable transitioning ML from being a novel, exploratory tool to becoming an integral part of the assessment
and design toolbox across multiple industries. Ultimately, the key to progress lies in fostering collaboration across
domains—bringing together data scientists, engineers, and domain experts—to develop trustworthy, scalable models
capable of addressing the pressing challenges of granular material applications.

                                          305. Limitations


  GNS is an efficient surrogate model for forward simulation. However, generalization beyond

training data may not perfectly replicate the high fidelity ground truth behaviors, resulting in some

inevitable error, as shown in figs. 12 and 16. To mitigate this, expanding the training dataset to

encompass a more comprehensive array of scenarios could help reduce the prediction error.

   While gradient checkpointing offers a workaround for the high memory demands associated with

reverse-mode AD in GNN, tracking the gradient over the GNN with large graphs is still expensive.

We evaluated peak memory usage during backpropagation across up to 400 forward computation

steps with increasing particles, as depicted in fig. 17. At around 20K particles, the backpropagation

process exceeds the memory capacity of our device (16 GB, RTX node at Frontera, TACC), failing.

Introducing checkpoints more frequently can reduce memory consumption; however, this strategy

requires additional computations for the forward pass, leading to a trade-off between memory

efficiency and computational overhead. Another strategy to alleviate memory constraints involves

partitioning the graph (C¸ataly¨urek et al., 2023) and employing multi-GPU processing. Our GNS

implementation (Kumar and Vantassel, 2022) supports efficient multi-GPU processing. However,

effectively partitioning large graphs and facilitating communication across these partitions in a

multi-GPU environment presents challenges and is the subject of active research.



6. Conclusion


   This study introduces an AD-based efficient framework for solving complex inverse problems

in granular flows using graph neural network-based simulators (GNS). By leveraging the compu-

tational efficiency, differentiability, and generalization capabilities of GNS, coupled with gradient-

based optimization through reverse-mode AD, our approach successfully identifies optimal param-

eters to achieve desired outcomes in diverse granular flow scenarios.

  We demonstrate the effectiveness of our methodology in solving single-parameter and multi-

parameter inverse analysis and design problems in granular flows. The single parameter optimiza-

tion achieves < 8.94% error in estimating ϕ compared to ϕtarget. In the multi-parameter case, the

initial velocity is inferred within 8.70e-4 MSE. For the design problem, our method identifies a rea-

sonable baffle arrangement with 1.89e-3 MSE, which is about an order of magnitude improved than

the initial guess (2.30e-2). Despite the test configurations being outside the training distribution,

our technique generalizes well, highlighting the flexibility of the methodology. Inverse analysis with

AD-GNS shows reasonable parameter estimations over a wide range of inverse problems. Never-

theless, the surrogate nature of GNS means some errors are inevitable compared to a high-fidelity

simulator. However, the result from our method provides useful information on parameters for

further analyses using high-fidelity solvers.

   The proposed AD-GNS framework solves inverse problems efficiently on a single GPU, achieving

151x speedups compared to forward high-fidelity simulators with finite difference gradients. Fur-

thermore, the integration of gradient checkpointing enables scaling to complex 3D dynamics over

hundreds of timesteps that would otherwise be infeasible due to the excessive memory consumption

for backpropagation.

    Overall, this study highlights the prospect of data-driven differentiable surrogates in inverse

modeling of granular flow hazards.

{"answer": "# Machine-learned surrogates for auger-powder calibration

**Bottom line.** For the described 3-mm-outlet doser, start with a **probabilistic emulator of measured DEM outputs**, not a pretrained particle simulator. A Gaussian process (GP), small neural network, or fitted response surface can map contact parameters and operating conditions directly to mass per revolution, tap release, afterflow, and no-flow probability. This is much cheaper to train than a full trajectory model and permits posterior uncertainty and targeted DEM runs. Particle graph simulators are promising if many related geometries or operating trajectories must eventually be simulated, but published speed and generalization results do **not** establish that an existing checkpoint predicts a tapped, intermittently flowing, SJKR-cohesive auger. Published granular examples also distinguish DEM-trained models from models trained on the material point method (MPM). (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000036, pqac-00000070)

## What has been demonstrated

| Approach | Training target and demonstrated scope | Generalization and relevance to the doser |
|---|---|---|
| **Particle graph simulators (GNS; “learning to simulate”)** | Construct nearby-particle edges; an encoder–message-passing processor–decoder predicts acceleration, followed by numerical position/velocity updates. Choi and Kumar trained a granular GNS on **MPM**, not DEM: 385 two-dimensional trajectories at five friction angles, 15°–45°, and 1,000 three-dimensional barrier trajectories. | Demonstrated different column configurations and barriers, and friction-angle-conditioned prediction within the studied setting. Their 2D training material had **fixed cohesion** of 0.1 kPa; this is not evidence for extrapolation over SJKR surface energy, rolling friction, moisture, or an auger outlet. (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000007, pqac-00000019) |
| **Mayr et al., Learning 3D Granular Flow / Boundary Graph Neural Networks (BGNN)** | **LIGGGHTS DEM** trajectories train a particle graph. Virtual nodes at nearby triangular-wall surfaces convey particle–wall distances and surface normals. Evaluations include hoppers, rotating drums, and moving-blade mixers; the earlier hopper study used 30 trajectories with varied wall angles, openings, and initial fills. Cohesive as well as noncohesive examples appear in the BGNN evaluation. | The authors tested **held-out changes to hopper outlet/wall angles and drum length**; Figure 5 displays predictions beside DEM ground truth for these out-of-distribution geometries. This is more pertinent to an auger than column collapse, but is **not** a test of a new contact law or reliable prediction of rare clogs. For one drum benchmark, 250,000 LIGGGHTS steps took **356 s on a CPU**, versus **158 s for 2,500 BGNN predictions on an A100**—different hardware and time resolution. (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000063, pqac-00000068) |
| **NeuralDEM, Alkin et al. (2025)** | A **DEM/CFD–DEM-trained field-based neural operator**: compress particle information into continuous fields and use interacting transformer-style branches for particle and, where applicable, fluid dynamics. Hopper data vary geometry and friction; a separate fluidized-bed model uses CFD–DEM. It predicts macroscopic drainage, transport, and mixing rather than requiring accurate individual-particle paths. | It handled withheld **combinations** of hopper angle and shear-cell friction angle within the studied range; this is parameter interpolation, not a verified new auger geometry or new SJKR physics. In its reported benchmarks, a 250,000-particle, 40-s hopper DEM run took **3 h on 16 CPU cores**, versus **1.4 s** for the fastest neural rollout on one GPU (**8 s** including all output points); a 500,000-particle fluidized-bed case took **6 h on 64 CPU cores**, versus **11 s** on one GPU. Training the fluidized-bed model used approximately **320 H100 GPU-hours**. These figures describe different hardware and exclude amortization of dataset generation. (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000014, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000023) |
| **Contact-memory graph networks (TRACE, 2026 preprint)** | Store evolving **contact-edge memory**, predict constrained normal/tangential forces, and train with single-step then rollout losses. Tested on 2D/3D column collapse against **MPM**, not an SJKR auger DEM. | Reports **8.9×–12.2×** speed relative to its MPM reference and improved deposit errors over graph baselines. Contact history is attractive for stop/start flow, but published tests do not demonstrate moisture, adhesive bonds, tapped walls, or inference of physical cohesion. (pqac-00000016) |
| **Low-dimensional DEM-output emulators** | Train directly on responses at deliberately chosen contact-parameter settings. Demonstrations include a quadratic D-optimal regression of repose angle, porosity, and flow rate for cohesive/free-flowing powders; a **symbolic-regression** metamodel fitted to **563 DEM parameter sets**, checked against 68 independent sets; and polynomial response surfaces for rotating-drum avalanche energies of AM powders. | Best matched to a small number of expensive auger outputs and Bayesian inversion. A fitted response surface is reliable only inside its sampled geometry, contact-model, environmental, and operating-condition domain; it does not automatically simulate particles or transfer to recoating. In the rotating-drum study, factor screening also eliminated weakly influential wall-contact parameters before fitting, illustrating why parameter identifiability should be assessed before expanding a design. (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000035, pqac-00000038) |

A **neural operator** learns a map between discretized fields, rather than rebuilding and stepping every grain-contact graph. NeuralDEM is a concrete granular example; it is not evidence that a generic Fourier neural operator, trained on unrelated fields, can resolve a 3-mm bridge or predict a zero-flow event. The granular-ML review specifically notes difficulties with changing particle contacts, solid-to-flowing transitions, and reconstructing physically admissible particle states from field representations. Thus, use a field operator if macroscopic fields over many operating conditions justify its training cost; retain contact-resolved DEM when clogging and tap-induced release determine the likelihood. (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000014, pqac-00000070)

## Inverse problems: what is known, and what is not

**Friction has been inverted with a differentiable graph simulator.** Choi and Kumar differentiated an MPM-trained GNS through a granular-column rollout and optimized friction angle against a target runout distance. Four held-out collapse cases gave inferred-angle errors **below 8.94%**; the authors report approximately **151×** faster optimization iterations than their MPM/finite-difference baseline. This estimates a continuum-model friction angle—not particle–particle sliding friction, wall friction, SJKR cohesion, or moisture from auger mass data. Differentiating long particle rollouts was memory-intensive and required checkpointing. (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000073)

**Cohesion-related and rolling parameters have been estimated with DEM response surrogates**, but an optimizer is not a Bayesian posterior. Katagiri and colleagues used GP-guided Bayesian optimization of a cohesion-related coefficient and rolling resistance against consolidation void ratio. A near-optimal result appeared within **12 optimization trials**; nevertheless, those calibrated parameters produced an **excessively cohesive spreading layer**. The authors attribute this to changed loading mechanics and stress scaling. Their GP guides evaluations toward an optimum; it does not by itself report a joint probability distribution of plausible physical parameters. For an actual parameter posterior, **GrainLearning** provides sequential Bayesian filtering of experimental time series against DEM runs and supports surrogate modeling as an alternative to repeatedly evaluating DEM. (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000037)

**Non-uniqueness is a substantive risk.** In a cohesive-powder study, different adhesion-energy/rolling-friction combinations reproduced the same repose angle, while matching unconfined yield strength called for a substantially different rolling-friction value. No single tested set reproduced both measurements consistently. A salt mass-per-revolution match without fitting is an excellent **forward check for that case**, but it is not evidence that the remaining powders’ contact parameters are identifiable from mean dose alone. (pqac-00000036, pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040)

## Recommended calibration and validation design

1. **Define the estimand as effective DEM parameters.** For each powder and batch, condition particle-size distribution, density, and measured moisture history; infer a *small, sensitivity-screened* subset of particle–particle sliding/rolling resistance, particle–PLA/PETG wall interaction, and SJKR cohesion. Treat fill level/packing history, powder shape, ambient humidity, and the tap impulse as recorded inputs or nuisance variables. Adhesive-energy and rolling coefficients depend on the chosen contact law and representation of particle shape; do not report them as uniquely measured intrinsic material constants. The finding that rolling friction can compensate for spherical representation of nonspherical grains reinforces this distinction. (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000036, pqac-00000066)
2. **Generate an auger-specific DEM design.** Sample physically plausible parameters and deliberately include both flowing and jammed regimes, each reservoir, low/high fill, tilt, 1–30 rpm, stop/start states, and housing taps. Export the *same balance-observable summaries* as in the laboratory, with replicate initial packings; reserve entire powder batches, operating conditions, and, if relevant, outlet geometries as held-out tests. A predictor of average mass per turn alone cannot be expected to learn afterflow or the no-flow fraction. The varied-parameter DEM datasets and out-of-distribution geometry tests in published work illustrate the need to include each intended axis of generalization in training and evaluation. (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000063, pqac-00000070)
3. **Fit a multi-output or linked likelihood.** A GP or small ensemble can emulate continuous mass-per-revolution, tap mass, and afterflow parameters; fit no-flow events with a Bernoulli/binomial likelihood and account for replicate variation. Compare posterior predictions to the **full incremental-mass traces**, not just their means. Include measurement noise, DEM-to-experiment discrepancy, and emulator uncertainty; acquire new DEM runs where posterior probability or uncertainty is high, especially near flow/no-flow transitions. These are proposed design choices for this doser, rather than published validation of an auger-specific surrogate. Bayesian filtering and documented cross-test failures motivate explicit uncertainty and independent checks. (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000070)
4. **Cross-check, do not force a universal flowability score.** Use **D7891 FT4 shear testing** and **D6773 ring shear** for constrained-strength information; **B213 Hall** and **B964 Carney** for funnel flow (including non-flow); **B212** apparent density and **B527** tap density for packing; **B214** sieving and **B822** light-scattering sizing for feed distribution. Include repose angle, documented humidity/conditioning and loss on drying. Report the actual apparatus, consolidation stress, sample preparation, and conditioning: these methods probe different stress and flow regimes. The source review’s summary table inconsistently groups some flow and density methods; its bibliography explicitly names **B964 as Carney *flow rate*** and **D7891 as Freeman powder *shear testing***, so those should not be silently relabeled as density or universal spreadability tests. (pqac-00000043, pqac-00000048, pqac-00000050, pqac-00000067)
5. **Measure spreadability separately.** For the AM-relevant metal powders, compare posterior-predictive rankings with a small recoater experiment at relevant blade/roller type, speeds and layer heights: image-based coverage and bare-patch frequency, layer mass/packing, thickness variability, and surface-height variation. Hulme-Smith and colleagues demonstrated inexpensive image-derived layer coverage over **50–200 mm/s** and **50–100 µm**; Yuasa and colleagues found AlSi10Mg surface-height variation increased markedly above **50 mm/s**, and powder-shape rankings changed at high speed. Angle of repose and FT4 basic flow energy can be informative correlates, but dosability through an auger, funnel discharge, and thin-layer recoating are *different operations*. The consolidation-to-spreading failure is direct evidence against declaring spreadability from a calibrated dosing fingerprint alone. (pqac-00000042, pqac-00000055, pqac-00000027)

At **26–30 CPU-min per revolution**, even 100 single-revolution DEM cases would require roughly **43–50 CPU-hours**, before initialization, extra turns, replicates, and tap/afterflow sequences. This is a planning calculation from the runtime supplied in the question, **not** a published benchmark. It favors factor screening, space-filling initial runs, adaptive acquisition, and a cheap summary-output emulator first. Use a wall-aware particle GNN later if those runs already produce sufficient resolved trajectories and the research question genuinely requires transfer between screw/outlet designs. The reported NeuralDEM inference speed should not be read as a prediction of its training or validation cost for this doser. (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000038, pqac-00000070)

## Public software and pretrained artifacts

- **NeuralDEM:** [github.com/Emmi-AI/NeuralDEM](https://github.com/Emmi-AI/NeuralDEM). The authors state that inference code, **pretrained model weights**, and one example trajectory for each hopper and fluidized-bed case are released; the complete approximately **3.2-TB** datasets are available on request. Those weights were trained for the published cases, not an auger. (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000061)
- **Choi–Kumar GNS and inverse examples:** [github.com/geoelements/gns](https://github.com/geoelements/gns) and [github.com/geoelements/gns-inverse-examples](https://github.com/geoelements/gns-inverse-examples), reported under MIT license. Their **training data and trained models** are deposited on DesignSafe; the paper lists dataset DOI **10.17603/DS2-4NQZ-S548** and inverse-example DOI **10.17603/DS2-0WJQ-0J84**. These are MPM-trained granular examples. (pqac-00000064, pqac-00000073)
- **Mayr BGNN:** [ml-jku.github.io/bgnn](https://ml-jku.github.io/bgnn/) is the documented project page with visualizations. The retrieved paper establishes this page, **not a verified downloadable pretrained checkpoint**; verify repository and license before planning reuse. (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000063)
- **TRACE:** [github.com/Data-Driven-Computational-Geotechnics/TRACE](https://github.com/Data-Driven-Computational-Geotechnics/TRACE) is documented as available code; a pretrained auger or DEM-contact-law checkpoint is **not documented**. (pqac-00000016)
- **GrainLearning:** an open-source Bayesian calibration/surrogate toolbox with published [JOSS software article](https://doi.org/10.21105/joss.06338) and [archived release](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.8352544). It is infrastructure for calibration, **not a pretrained powder-flow predictor**. (pqac-00000065, pqac-00000074)

**Assessment:** Existing open implementations provide useful architectures, calibration software, and some pretrained *benchmark* weights. None of the cited evidence establishes a transferable pretrained model for this doser’s PLA/PETG walls, rotating helix, SJKR adhesion, taps, and intermittent milligram-scale discharge. The experimentally defensible route is an auger-specific, uncertainty-aware inverse emulator, independently challenged by shear, packing, size/moisture, and actual recoating observations. (pqac-00000036, pqac-00000061, pqac-00000070)"}

state.question: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. What machine-learned surrogate simulators exist for granular flow (graph-network simulators such as GNS and 'learning to simulate', neural operators, Gaussian-process or neural-network emulators of DEM outputs), how are they trained from DEM data, how well do they generalize to new geometries and contact parameters, and have they been used for inverse problems such as estimating friction or cohesion from observed flow? Which open-source implementations and pretrained models exist?

contexts.context: The excerpt provides a concrete granular-flow surrogate example based on a Graph Neural Network-based Simulator (GNS), but it does not cover the requested DEM-specific NeuralDEM/neural-operator, GP/NN response-surface, thesis, TRACE, powder-calibration, inverse-estimation, repository, or pretrained-weight details. In the reported example, Material Point Method (MPM) simulations—not DEM simulations—generate trajectories for training. The modeled problem is granular-column collapse, with inputs including column geometry (aspect ratios 0.5–4.0), friction angles (15°–45°), and boundary conditions. The main quantity of interest is runout distance, while material-point positions are tracked over time; simulations also represent column-collapse dynamics and barrier interactions. The GNS uses a graph representation with an encoder, a processor performing 10 message-passing steps, and a decoder. An updater applies Euler integration to position updates, injecting domain knowledge and focusing learning on unknown dynamics. Connectivity radius is cited as a key hyperparameter, with example values of 0.030 m in 2D and 0.025 m in 3D. Gaussian-noise augmentation is used to improve long-term stability, and training uses Adam with learning-rate decay on multi-GPU hardware. During inference, the initial granular geometry, material properties, and boundary conditions are encoded as a graph whose vertices represent material points.

snippets: Graph neural networks (GNNs) [152, 90] provide an effective framework for modelling the dynamics of granular materials and particle systems.

By representing granular assemblies as graphs, with nodes corresponding to particles and edges encoding their interactions, GNNs can learn the underlying interaction laws governing particle motion in a permutation-invariant manner.

GNS takes the current state of the granular domain (particle positions, velocities, boundaries) as input and predicts the acceleration of each particle, which is then numerically integrated to model the time evolution of the particles.
Trained on high-fidelity simulations, GNS demonstrates accurate predictions while being orders of magnitude faster than traditional numerical methods.
Applications of GNS for particulate systems involve granular column collapse [39], granular flows with complex boundaries [117] and solving inverse problems [94, 40, 83].
However, a major drawback of GNNs is that their computational complexity grows with the number of particles as the number of nodes in the graph grows accordingly.

snippets: Our concept workflow mainly encompasses three stages, namely data simulation, understanding and preparation, modelling and evaluation.
The simulation workflow begins with data preparation and understanding using physics-based granular material models.
Techniques such as transfer learning and active learning can improve efficiency.
The Discrete Element Method (DEM) is used to simulate the compression of a RVE filled with grains to a certain porosity.
These simulations vary in contact parameters and are saved at regular time intervals.
A training dataset is then created, covering the evolution of these QoIs over the chosen loading paths for a wide range of contact parameters [37] and microstructures [110].

contexts.context: The excerpt provides Choi’s GNS learned-surrogate architecture and training-data details, but does not contain the requested information about Fransen, TRACE, NeuralDEM/neural operators, GP/NN DEM response surfaces, open-source repositories, or pretrained weights. GNS represents granular media as a particle/region interaction graph: node states include position, velocity, boundary distance, and material properties. Its dynamics approximator has an encoder–processor–decoder design. The encoder maps the current state to a latent graph; a GNN processor passes messages along edges to represent particle interactions and exchanges; the decoder predicts particle dynamics, interpreted as acceleration. An update function advances the state, analogous to explicit Euler integration, producing sequential rollouts. Training minimizes mean-squared error between MPM-generated ground-truth and predicted accelerations. The 2D Flow2D dataset contains 385 trajectories, spanning five friction angles (15°, 22.5°, 30°, 37.5°, and 45°), with varying mass size, position, and velocity. The 3D Obstacle3D dataset contains 1,000 barrier-interaction trajectories, varying cuboid mass dimensions, initial velocities, and one to three barriers. Table 3.1 specifies Mohr–Coulomb materials, density 1,800 kg/m³, Young’s modulus 2 MPa, Poisson ratio 0.3; Flow2D additionally uses cohesion 0.1 kPa and tension cutoff 0.05 kPa, while Obstacle3D uses friction angle 35° and no cohesion. Differentiability enables gradient-based inverse estimation, including material properties, initial conditions, and barrier placement, but the excerpt does not report a completed friction/cohesion estimation result.

contexts.context: The excerpt documents Mayr et al.’s Learning 3D Granular Flow surrogate, trained on discrete-element-method trajectories generated with the open-source LIGGGHTS simulator. The target applications include complex 3D granular flows in industrially relevant systems such as rotating drums and hoppers; the excerpt does not mention Alkin NeuralDEM or TRACE. The model is a graph neural network using an encoder–processor–decoder time-transition architecture. It predicts particle acceleration at the next timestep, then updates velocity and position using explicit equations. Relative positional encoding is used. For nontrivial 3D boundaries, the method dynamically inserts virtual boundary nodes when real particles are close to a triangular mesh. Node features distinguish real and virtual particles; virtual nodes additionally carry the triangular surface normal, while real particles use null normal vectors. Boundary proximity is represented by the minimum distance from a particle center to the closest point on mesh triangles. The network is trained to handle particle–particle and particle–boundary interactions and to be invariant to normal-vector orientation. The provided pages do not specify dataset counts or sizes, physical-parameter ranges, unseen-geometry test results, speedups, limitations in quantitative detail, or public GitHub/checkpoint URLs. snippets: Graph neural networks (GNNs) [152, 90] provide an effective framework for modelling the dynamics of granular materials and particle systems.

By representing granular assemblies as graphs, with nodes corresponding to particles and edges encoding their interactions, GNNs can learn the underlying interaction laws governing particle motion in a permutation-invariant manner.
GNS takes the current state of the granular domain (particle positions, velocities, boundaries) as input and predicts the acceleration of each particle
Trained on high-fidelity simulations, GNS demonstrates accurate predictions while being orders of magnitude faster than traditional numerical methods.
However, a major drawback of GNNs is that their computational complexity grows with the number of particles

contexts.context: The excerpt describes Alkin et al.’s NeuralDEM as an end-to-end deep-learning surrogate for computationally intensive DEM and coupled CFD–DEM simulations, intended for fast, flexible, real-time modeling of industrial-scale particulate flows. Its two central ideas are a physics representation and multi-branch neural operators. The Lagrangian DEM discretization is represented as an underlying continuous field, while macroscopic behavior is modeled through auxiliary fields. Example inputs include particle displacement, particle mixing, solid fraction, and particle transport. Different physical phases are assigned separate main branches implemented with transformer-style neural operators: in a particle–fluid example, one branch predicts particle displacements and another predicts fluid velocities and pressures, with frequent information exchange coupling the branches. More generally, the neural operator learns a function-to-function map using encoder, approximator, and decoder components, trained by supervised learning with a discretized mean-squared-error loss. The motivation for large time steps is that local flow evolution is mainly controlled by nearby bounded regions, a behavior likened to transformer attention. This excerpt does not provide dataset counts or sizes, physical parameter ranges, unseen-geometry tests, measured speedups, limitations, or public GitHub/checkpoint links.

contexts.context: The excerpt documents TRACE, but contains no information about the Mayr Learning 3D Granular Flow and Boundary Graph Neural Networks model or Alkin NeuralDEM, nor does it establish that TRACE was DEM-trained. TRACE is a spatiotemporal contact-memory graph simulator in which contact-edge memories are updated through attention-based message passing and a GRU. A time-invariant edge-identity dictionary retains memory when contacts form, break, and rearrange. Its physics-structured decoder predicts normal and tangential contact forces, imposes the Coulomb friction constraint, and enforces equal-and-opposite internal forces. Training uses single-step pretraining followed by autoregressive rollout fine-tuning. Evaluation covers 2D and 3D granular column-collapse benchmarks; benchmark particle counts, dataset sizes, physical-parameter ranges, and tests on unseen geometries are not provided in the excerpt. Reported results include stable long-horizon rollouts, near-zero particle interpenetration, 31–62% lower long-rollout position error, 58–89% lower final-deposit error versus GNS and NMGNS, and 12.2×/8.9× speedups over an MPM reference solver in 2D/3D. The excerpt gives the public repository link but no checkpoint link. It does not state broader limitations beyond the challenge of preserving contact history and the listed benchmark scope.

contexts.context: The excerpt documents Mayr et al.’s Learning 3D Granular Flow approach as a graph neural network surrogate for 3D granular-flow simulations, including particle–particle and particle–boundary interactions. Boundary geometry is represented using virtual boundary particles/nodes, with node features indicating whether a node is real or virtual and, for boundary nodes, the triangular surface normal. Particle proximity to the boundary is computed as the minimum Euclidean distance from the particle center to the closest point on a mesh triangle, obtained by constrained point–triangle optimization. To improve boundary learning despite fewer particle–boundary examples, the model emphasizes type and normal-vector features and sorts both positive and negative normal orientations using a partial-order function, aiming for orientation-invariant predictions. The reported applications are a hopper and a rotating drum. Hopper training data comprises 30 simulation trajectories spanning different wall angles α, hole sizes, and initial filling distributions; the drum uses a y-axis rotation and a rotated resting-drum filling initialization. Results show qualitative agreement in particle-averaged positions, time- and particle-averaged flows, and mixing entropy, although long-term trajectories diverge because of chaotic behavior. The excerpt does not provide dataset particle counts, detailed physical-parameter ranges, unseen-geometry tests, speed benchmarks, LIGGGHTS details, checkpoint files, or GitHub links.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides Mayr et al.’s Boundary Graph Neural Network (BGNN) details, but does not document the Alkin NeuralDEM model or TRACE contact-memory model. BGNNs address particle–boundary interactions by dynamically modifying graph edges, augmenting node features, and inserting virtual nodes. They were evaluated on complex 3D granular-flow scenarios involving hoppers, rotating drums, and mixers, including moving geometries and rotating blades. The model reportedly reproduced flows within simulation uncertainties for hundreds of thousands of timesteps, while keeping particles inside geometric objects without handcrafted boundary conditions or restrictions. A stated dataset trajectory contains 3,408 particles and requires approximately 2 GB of GPU memory for one forward pass; speed improvements in the reported simple setups are attributed substantially to GPU parallelization. The authors identify potential limitations and extensions: material behavior involving higher Young’s moduli may require improved predictions, and a velocity-dependent cutoff radius could capture imminent particle–boundary interactions at larger spatial distances. They also suggest exploiting granular-flow symmetries and geometries. The documented public project page is https://ml-jku.github.io/bgnn/. contexts.context: The excerpt documents Alkin et al.’s NeuralDEM, a DEM-trained deep-learning surrogate for industrial granular and coupled fluid–particle flows. Its architecture uses multi-branch neural operators inspired by multi-modal diffusion transformers (MMDiT), together with a compressed Eulerian, field-based representation of the underlying Lagrangian DEM discretization. Auxiliary continuous fields represent macroscopic processes such as mixing and transport, while repeated interactions between physics phases support multiphysics modeling. The model is conditioned on macroscopic quantities and boundary conditions, including inflow velocity and internal friction angle, rather than requiring finely tuned microscopic DEM parameters, and is designed to remain stable over longer timesteps. The reported evaluation uses separately trained models for two lab-scale industrial cases: slow, pseudo-steady hoppers with varying hopper angles, internal friction angles, and flow regimes; and fast, transient gas-solid fluidized-bed reactors with varying inflow velocities. Training simulations contained up to half a million particles. The excerpt states that the models reproduce macroscopic quantities including drainage times, residence times, and mixing indices, extrapolate dynamics over long horizons, and reduce simulation costs by several orders of magnitude. It does not provide exact runtime values, explicit unseen-geometry test results, known limitations beyond the stated lab-scale evaluation and anticipated scaling, or public GitHub/checkpoint links; only the DOI is documented.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a graph-based learned simulator for 3D hopper particle flow, emphasizing geometry generalization through orientation-invariant wall-normal features. It compares: no normals (V1), one mesh-order normal (V2), and both orientations (V3). V3 significantly improves test Earth Mover’s Distance over V1 (p=2.42×10⁻⁴) and V2 (p=1.50×10⁻³), suggesting better generalization despite limited training benefit. A toy ReLU network learned plane reflection only when inverted normals were handled via a partial ordering, \(f_o(n)=\sum_{i=1}^3 3^{i-1}(\mathrm{sgn}(n_i)+1)\). No inverse calibration or pretrained implementation is reported.
contexts.question: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. What machine-learned surrogate simulators exist for granular flow (graph-network simulators such as GNS and 'learning to simulate', neural operators, Gaussian-process or neural-network emulators of DEM outputs), how are they trained from DEM data, how well do they generalize to new geometries and contact parameters, and have they been used for inverse problems such as estimating friction or cohesion from observed flow? Which open-source implementations and pretrained models exist?

NeuralDEM was trained using data from 3-second simulations and evaluated on substantially longer rollouts. For a 250,000-particle hopper case, conventional DEM required 3 hours on 16 CPU cores for 40 seconds of simulation, whereas the fastest NeuralDEM model reproduced the rollout in 1.4 seconds on one GPU; processing all output points took 8 seconds. For a 500,000-particle fluidized-bed reactor, CFD-DEM required 6 hours on 64 CPU cores, while NeuralDEM reproduced the behavior in 11 seconds on one GPU. The fluidized-bed model captured chaotic bubble dynamics, transitions in flow patterns, long-term averages, and mass conservation within a 1.5% error margin. NeuralDEM can be conditioned on macroscopic friction angle and flow-function measurements rather than microscopic DEM parameters; hopper draining-time error increased from 0.19 seconds with microscopic parameters to 0.4 seconds with macroscopic characteristics. The article also notes that the tested cases were smaller and simpler than real industrial processes.

contexts.context: El-Kassem et al. (2020/2021) conducted a systematic DEM parameter study for free-flowing and cohesive powders, examining Young’s modulus, particle size, particle–particle restitution, static friction, rolling friction, and cohesion energy density against bulk responses including angle of repose and porosity. For cohesive powder, the overall trends were similar, but particle stiffness negatively affected angle of repose and cohesion energy density influenced all responses; cohesion increased the influence of stiffness on some responses, including angle of repose. Coarse-graining particle size did not affect angle of repose in either powder study. The authors used a quadratic D-optimal design and regression-based prediction models, validated against experiments. For cohesive powder validation, the predicted angle of repose was 40° versus an experimental value of 40.8° (2% deviation), and predicted porosity was 56.23% versus 54.84% (−2.47% deviation).

contexts.context: El-Kassem et al. (2020/2021) investigated DEM parameter sensitivity for free-flowing and cohesive powders using an optimized quadratic D-optimal design and multivariate regression analysis, with experimental validation based on angle-of-repose tests. The study examined six microscopic DEM inputs: static friction, rolling friction, restitution, particle size, Young’s modulus, and cohesion energy density. Its macroscopic outputs included angle of repose, porosity, mass flow rate, translational kinetic energy, and computation time. For cohesive powders, rolling friction had a substantial influence on the angle of repose, whereas static friction and particle size played comparatively minor roles. Across both powder types, porosity was strongly affected by the static and rolling friction coefficients. These findings are relevant when comparing DEM calibration strategies: they indicate that friction parameters do not necessarily affect all macroscopic observables equally, and that calibration against angle of repose may emphasize different parameters than calibration against porosity or other flow responses. contexts.context: Lupo et al. (2021) describe two DEM calibration approaches relevant to comparing angle-of-repose and shear-based calibration. For static angle of repose, particles are generated randomly in a virtual hopper, fall through the hopper opening, and deposit on a freshly created layer of the same powder. Particle generation stops once a visible heap forms, and the angle is measured after the particles become steady. The simulated hopper is a truncated cone with base radii of 100 and 400 µm and a height of 1 mm; the simulation used 40 CPUs and required approximately 8 hours. For cohesive powder strength, the authors explain that unconstrained/unconfined yield strength is commonly obtained indirectly from shear testing through a Mohr-circle construction and flow-function analysis. Rather than simulate the cumbersome shear tester, they use an idealized uniaxial DEM experiment and compare the simulated strength fc(sim) with the experimentally inferred value fc(exp). The setup minimizes wall effects by assigning particle-wall sliding and rolling friction coefficients of 10^-4 during compaction. It includes powder-bed generation, compaction, relaxation, and unconstrained compression; gravity is set to zero. The excerpt does not provide numerical inverse-optimization iterations, emulator architecture, or evidence of a direct conflict between angle-of-repose and shear calibration.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes El-Kassem et al.’s DEM parametric study using the angle of repose (AoR) as the principal powder-flow response. In the laboratory procedure, 5 g of powder was discharged by gravity from a stainless-steel funnel into a glass container to form a pile; each powder test was repeated five times, and the mean measured angle was used as its AoR. The authors state that the AoR depends on interparticulate friction and is commonly used both to characterize powder flowability and to calibrate DEM parameters. Their parameter study used a D-optimal experimental design to reduce the number of simulations while retaining significance and to identify combinations of microscopic input parameters for testing. The DEM formulation employs the soft-particle approach, Hertz–Mindlin contact forces, and separate normal and tangential elastic/damping terms. The excerpt also introduces rolling friction as a contact-dependent interaction in addition to sliding friction. It emphasizes that rolling friction is particularly important because it compensates for representing real, nonspherical particles with spherical DEM particles; thus, it can materially affect simulated pile formation and AoR calibration. contexts.context: The excerpt provides the Richter and Will (2021) global metamodel details. The metamodels were trained using 563 parameter sets generated by the FSSF-f algorithm; originally 600 simulations were performed, but some results were discarded because of simulation crashes. Accuracy was validated on a separate dataset containing 68 parameter sets generated through random sampling. The response variables were shear angle (ϕ) and bulk density (ρ), extracted automatically from simulation output. Shear angle was determined by evaluating particle coordinates at the end of the simulation and fitting a linear regression through the uppermost particles, while bulk density was calculated from particle mass and box volume. The excerpt identifies the scalar-emulator approach as symbolic regression rather than a conventional fixed-form regression model. Specifically, it uses genetic programming (GP), implemented with gplearn, which evolves mathematical expression trees through selection, crossover, and mutation. The GP population size was 5,000 individuals, with a parsimony coefficient of 0.001 to penalize overly large expressions and control bloat. The function set included addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, square root, logarithm, exponential, and hyperbolic tangent; trigonometric functions were excluded because periodic behavior was not expected and their use could promote overfitting. contexts.context: The excerpt describes Choi and Kumar’s single-parameter inverse problem for recovering the granular material friction angle from a target runout distance. AD-GNS performs a forward simulation for a trial friction angle, defines the loss as the squared difference between simulated and target runout, and computes the friction-angle gradient using reverse-mode automatic differentiation. Gradient descent updates the angle until the squared error is below 0.0005. Four granular-column-collapse scenarios were selected, spanning aspect ratios from 0.5 to 2.0 and involving 3,200 particles per simulation. The optimization used a learning rate of 500 and initialized the friction angle at 30 degrees. According to the excerpt, convergence occurred in only a few iterations, with recovered friction-angle errors below 8.94%. The passage also notes that the GNS had not been trained on these inverse problems, emphasizing adaptability. Gradient checkpointing was required because ordinary reverse-mode differentiation exceeded available 40 GB GPU memory after only 3–4 timesteps for approximately 3,000 particles; checkpointing reduced memory by storing selected states and recomputing discarded states during backpropagation. The excerpt does not provide detailed iteration counts, discuss a fixed-cohesion limitation, or contain information about the other referenced emulator, surrogate, calibration, rolling-friction/porosity, or JKR-cohesion studies.

contexts.context: Lupo et al. (2021) investigate DEM calibration for cohesive particles in selective laser sintering powder spreading. Their bulk-calibration procedure seeks values for two DEM parameters: interfacial adhesive surface energy and coefficient of rolling friction. The calibration compares two experimental bulk measurements—angle of repose and unconfined yield strength—with corresponding simulations: a reproduced angle-of-repose test and an idealized uniaxial test for unconfined yield strength. The modeled particles are spheres using the Hertz–Mindlin contact model with JKR adhesion. The key numerical conclusion relevant to the question is that a single bulk-calibration approach could not produce parameter values giving results consistent with both bulk-property evaluations simultaneously. The authors therefore recommend preferentially using direct methods to estimate surface energy, such as approaches based on interparticle-force evaluation, rather than relying only on bulk-property matching. This excerpt does not contain information about Sani et al. contexts.context: This excerpt describes Katagiri et al.’s DEM parameter-identification study, which optimized two parameters: the cohesion-related parameter k and the rolling-friction coefficient μr (mr). Preliminary consolidation analyses supplied five results as prior information, after which Bayesian optimization was conducted over 12 trials. The search ranges were k = 10^2–10^5 J/m3 and mr = 0.05–0.7. The selected near-optimal parameters were k = 47,500 J/m3 and mr = 0.5, producing a simulated void ratio of 0.776 versus the experimental value of 0.783. A near-optimal result appeared by the fifth trial, although later trials did not necessarily improve it. The optimization used a Gaussian-process regression prediction model, updated iteratively using accumulated simulation results, to explore sparsely sampled regions of parameter space. The excerpt therefore supports distinguishing Bayesian optimization with a Gaussian-process surrogate from a neural-network surrogate, and from the posterior distribution itself: the GP is the predictive surrogate, while Bayesian optimization uses that model to select subsequent evaluations. The surrogate comprises three multi-input, single-output polynomial models, one for each response: break energy, rest energy, and avalanche energy. contexts.context: The excerpt provides information only about Lupo et al.’s DEM calibration, not Sani et al. (2026) or Katagiri. For the angle-of-repose calibration, the authors identify a logarithmic relationship between cohesion energy Γ and particle–particle rolling friction µR,P−P: µR,P−P = −0.032 ln Γ − 0.167. Multiple parameter pairs along this curve reproduce the experimental angle, so the angle-of-repose calibration is non-unique. The authors regard Γ values between 10−5 and 5 × 10−3 J/m² as candidate values; Γ = 10−2 J/m² gives a less satisfactory angle-of-repose prediction. Separately, calibration against unconﬁned yield strength finds only one matching pair within the tested range: Γ = 10−2 J/m² and µR,P−P = 0.326, producing fc = 141 ± 7 Pa, matching the experimentally extrapolated value of about 141 Pa. Thus, this excerpt supports a distinction between angle-of-repose calibration, which admits multiple equivalent parameter pairs, and yield-strength calibration, which yields one identified pair. contexts.context: Hulme-Smith et al. evaluated powder spreadability for additive manufacturing using image analysis of deposited layers. A fixed camera and two LED arrays were used; the LEDs operated at full intensity with a 5000 K light temperature, while room lights were switched off although ambient light sources remained. Images were processed by color-channel subtraction and automated thresholding to identify powder against the steel plate. The analysis quantified three geometric metrics: coverage of the available test area, coverage within an automatically determined convex hull, and coverage within a bounding box. Tests varied recoater speed and layer thickness, including 50 µm layers. Powder C produced the best spreading performance, covering the greatest area and filling the largest fractions of its convex hull and bounding box; Powder B performed worst. For Powder C, coverage generally increased with recoater speed, whereas all three metrics decreased with speed for Powder B. Powder A showed no strong speed relationship. Hall and Carney funnel results were consistent with these observations: A and B did not flow through either funnel, while C flowed readily. Rheometry also ranked C as best and B as worst, but the authors cautioned that additional testing was needed because powders A and C had similar specific energies. The method therefore provides comparative, process-specific spreadability information, but does not establish a universal standard or eliminate sensitivity to lighting, image segmentation, recoater conditions, and layer thickness.

It reports that Hausner ratio is inadequate for fine metal powders: many appear freely flowing by H < 1.25 despite poor optical flowability. Interparticle forces, particle-size distribution, and particle shape are important, with fine particles reducing flowability through a higher cohesive granular Bond number. Avalanche angle and surface-fractal measurements can capture these effects, but their mean values alone are insufficient; distributions, including D10/D50/D90, span, and skewness, provide more useful information. contexts.context: This excerpt is directly relevant to the spreadability and metal additive-manufacturing portions of the question, but it does not provide verification details for the listed ASTM standards or results from the other cited studies. Hulme-Smith, Hari, and Mellin emphasize that thin-layer formation is critical in powder-bed additive manufacturing because inconsistent layer thickness or density degrades build quality. They distinguish spreadability from conventional flowability: although Hall, Carney, and FT4-type flowability measurements can be recorded, flowability is not necessarily correlated with spreading performance. The paper proposes an automated, relatively low-cost image-analysis method using a thin-film applicator, adjustable doctor blade, fixed camera, controlled lighting, and ImageJ processing. The procedure thresholds powder against the substrate, measures covered area, convex-hull area, and bounding-box area, and calculates area ratios as quantitative spreading metrics. Three powders were tested over recoater speeds of 50–200 mm/s and nominal layer heights of 50, 70, and 100 µm. The excerpt therefore supports a caveat that standard flowability, density, or other powder tests should not automatically be treated as direct spreadability measures. It also provides a reproducible framework for relating powder coverage geometry to layer thickness and spreading speed.

contexts.context: The excerpt verifies several requested standards and provides important applicability caveats. For tapped density, it cites MPIF Standard 46, ASTM B527-20, and ISO 3953; tapping should use a calibrated mechanical machine, a graduated cylinder, and a documented, periodically rechecked tap count. For apparent density, it identifies MPIF Standards 4 (Hall apparatus) and 28 (Carney funnel), with ASTM B213 associated with Hall measurements. The Carney method uses a 5 mm orifice, a known-volume density cup, and levelling before weighing. ASTM D7891 is identified as the wall-friction test used with the Freeman Technology FT4; the FT4 also measures dynamic, shear, bulk, flow, aeration, and compressibility properties. FT4 interpretation requires caution because results depend on the flow regime and parameters should not be interpreted in isolation. ASTM D6393-14 (Carr Indices) covers cohesion, angle of repose, bulk density, and dispersibility, but is intended for free-flowing or moderately cohesive powders and granular materials up to 2 mm that pass through a 6–8 mm nozzle. Its angle-of-repose method is mainly suited to larger particles such as sands and is therefore less widely used in L-PBF research.
